title: Appendicitis – Pathogenesis
content: Lymphoid hyperplasia or a faecolith leads to obstruction of the appendiceal lumen, followed by gut organisms invading the appendix wall, resulting in oedema, ischaemia and potentially perforation.

title: Appendicitis – Epidemiology
content: Most common acute abdominal condition requiring surgery. Can occur at any age but is most common in young people aged 10-20 years.

title: Appendicitis – Pain migration pattern
content: Peri-umbilical abdominal pain (visceral stretching of appendix lumen, as appendix is a midgut structure) radiating to the right iliac fossa due to localised parietal peritoneal inflammation. The migration of pain from centre to right iliac fossa has been shown to be one of the strongest indicators of appendicitis.

title: Appendicitis – Pain characteristics on movement
content: Patients often report the pain being worse on coughing or going over speed bumps. Children typically cannot hop on the right leg due to the pain.

title: Appendicitis – Vomiting pattern
content: Vomit once or twice but marked and persistent vomiting is unusual.

title: Appendicitis – Diarrhoea presentation
content: Diarrhoea is rare. However, pelvic appendicitis may cause localised rectal irritation resulting in some loose stools. A pelvic abscess may also cause diarrhoea.

title: Appendicitis – Temperature characteristics
content: Mild pyrexia is common with temperature usually 37.5-38°C. Higher temperatures are more typical of conditions like mesenteric adenitis.

title: Appendicitis – Anorexia
content: Anorexia is very common. It is very unusual for patients with appendicitis to be hungry.

title: Appendicitis – Typical symptom triad
content: Around 50% of patients have the typical symptoms of anorexia, peri-umbilical pain and nausea followed by more localised right lower quadrant pain.

title: Appendicitis – Examination findings in perforation
content: Generalised peritonitis if perforation has occurred or localised peritonism with rebound and percussion tenderness, guarding and rigidity.

title: Appendicitis – Retrocaecal presentation
content: Retrocaecal appendicitis may have relatively few signs.

title: Appendicitis – Digital rectal examination findings
content: Digital rectal examination may reveal boggy sensation if pelvic abscess is present, or even right-sided tenderness with a pelvic appendix.

title: Appendicitis – Rovsing's sign
content: Palpation in the left iliac fossa causes pain in the right iliac fossa. Now thought to be of limited value.

title: Appendicitis – Psoas sign
content: Pain on extending hip if retrocaecal appendix is present.

title: Appendicitis – Diagnostic criteria
content: Typically raised inflammatory markers coupled with compatible history and examination findings should be enough to justify appendicectomy.

title: Appendicitis – Leucocytosis
content: A neutrophil-predominant leucocytosis is seen in 80-90% of cases.

title: Appendicitis – Urine analysis findings
content: Useful to exclude pregnancy in women, renal colic and urinary tract infection. In patients with appendicitis, urinalysis may show mild leucocytosis but no nitrites.

title: Appendicitis – Imaging indications
content: There are no definite rules on the use of imaging and its use is often determined by the patient's gender, age, body habitus and the likelihood of appendicitis.

title: Appendicitis – Ultrasound indications
content: Ultrasound is useful in females where pelvic organ pathology is suspected. Although it is not always possible to visualise the appendix on ultrasound, the presence of free fluid (always pathological in males) should raise suspicion. It is also useful in children as it avoids radiation exposure and has good diagnostic accuracy in paediatrics.

title: Appendicitis – CT imaging role
content: Contrast-enhanced CT imaging is widely used in adult patients with suspected appendicitis, particularly when the diagnosis is unclear. Ultrasound may still be useful first-line for female patients to exclude gynaecological pathology.

title: Appendicitis – Surgical approach
content: Appendicectomy can be performed via either an open or laparoscopic approach. Laparoscopic appendicectomy is now the treatment of choice.

title: Appendicitis – Prophylactic antibiotics
content: Administration of prophylactic intravenous antibiotics reduces wound infection rates.

title: Appendicitis – Management of perforation
content: Patients with perforated appendicitis (typical around 15-20%) require copious abdominal lavage.

title: Appendicitis – Management of appendix mass
content: Patients without peritonitis who have an appendix mass should receive broad-spectrum antibiotics and consideration given to performing an interval appendicectomy.

title: Appendicitis – Differential diagnosis in older patients
content: Be wary in the older patients who may have either an underlying caecal malignancy or perforated sigmoid diverticular disease.

title: Appendicitis – Conservative management with antibiotics
content: Trials have looked at the use of intravenous antibiotics alone in the treatment of appendicitis. The evidence currently suggests that whilst this is successful in the majority of patients, it is associated with a longer hospital stay and up to 20% of patients go on to have an appendicectomy within 12 months.

title: Cholecystitis – Definition
content: Inflammation of the gallbladder.

title: Cholecystitis – Calculous pathophysiology
content: Develops secondary to gallstones in 90% of patients (acute calculous cholecystitis).

title: Cholecystitis – Acalculous cholecystitis
content: The remaining 10% of cases are referred to as acalculous cholecystitis, typically seen in hospitalised and severely ill patients. Multifactorial pathophysiology includes gallbladder stasis, hypoperfusion and infection. Associated with high morbidity and mortality rates.

title: Cholecystitis – Acalculous in immunosuppressed patients
content: In immunosuppressed patients it may develop secondary to Cryptosporidium or cytomegalovirus.

title: Cholecystitis – Right upper quadrant pain
content: Right upper quadrant pain which may radiate to the right shoulder.

title: Cholecystitis – Fever and systemic upset
content: Fever and signs of systemic upset.

title: Cholecystitis – Murphy's sign
content: Murphy's sign on examination: inspiratory arrest upon palpation of the right upper quadrant.

title: Cholecystitis – Liver function tests
content: Liver function tests are typically normal.

title: Cholecystitis – Mirizzi syndrome
content: Deranged LFTs may indicate Mirizzi syndrome - a gallstone impacted in the distal cystic duct causing extrinsic compression of the common bile duct.

title: Cholecystitis – First-line investigation
content: Ultrasound is the first-line investigation of choice.

title: Cholecystitis – HIDA scan indication
content: If the diagnosis remains unclear then cholescintigraphy (HIDA scan) may be used.

title: Cholecystitis – HIDA scan mechanism
content: Technetium-labelled HIDA (hepatobiliary iminodiacetic acid) is injected IV and taken up selectively by hepatocytes and excreted into bile. In acute cholecystitis there is cystic duct obstruction (secondary to oedema associated with inflammation or an obstructing stone) and hence the gallbladder will not be visualised.

title: Cholecystitis – Antibiotic treatment
content: Intravenous antibiotics.

title: Cholecystitis – Timing of cholecystectomy
content: NICE now recommend early laparoscopic cholecystectomy, within 1 week of diagnosis. Previously, surgery was delayed for several weeks until the inflammation has subsided.

title: Cholecystitis – Management in pregnancy
content: Pregnant women should also proceed to early laparoscopic cholecystectomy - this reduces the chances of maternal-fetal complications.

title: Acute pancreatitis – Common causes
content: Usually due to alcohol or gallstones.

title: Acute pancreatitis – Pathophysiology
content: Autodigestion of pancreatic tissue by the pancreatic enzymes, leading to necrosis.

title: Acute pancreatitis – Epigastric pain characteristics
content: Severe epigastric pain that may radiate through to the back.

title: Acute pancreatitis – Vomiting
content: Vomiting is common.

title: Acute pancreatitis – Examination findings
content: Examination may reveal epigastric tenderness, ileus and low-grade fever.

title: Acute pancreatitis – Cullen's and Grey-Turner's signs
content: Periumbilical discolouration (Cullen's sign) and flank discolouration (Grey-Turner's sign) is described but rare.

title: Acute pancreatitis – Purtscher retinopathy
content: Ischaemic (Purtscher) retinopathy may cause temporary or permanent blindness.

title: Acute pancreatitis – Serum amylase findings
content: Raised in 75% of patients, typically greater than 3 times the upper limit of normal. Levels do not correlate with disease severity. Specificity for pancreatitis is around 90%.

title: Acute pancreatitis – Other causes of raised amylase
content: Other causes of raised amylase include pancreatic pseudocyst, mesenteric infarct, perforated viscus, acute cholecystitis, and diabetic ketoacidosis.

title: Acute pancreatitis – Serum lipase
content: More sensitive and specific than serum amylase. It also has a longer half-life than amylase and may be useful for late presentations greater than 24 hours.

title: Acute pancreatitis – Diagnosis without imaging
content: A diagnosis of acute pancreatitis can be made without imaging if characteristic pain plus amylase/lipase greater than 3 times normal level.

title: Acute pancreatitis – Role of ultrasound
content: Early ultrasound imaging is important to assess the aetiology as this may affect management, for example patients with gallstones or biliary obstruction.

title: Acute pancreatitis – CT imaging
content: Other imaging options include contrast-enhanced CT.

title: Acute pancreatitis – Severity scoring systems
content: Several scoring systems are used to identify cases of severe pancreatitis which may require intensive care management, including the Ranson score, Glasgow score and APACHE II.

title: Acute pancreatitis – Factors indicating severe disease
content: Common factors indicating severe pancreatitis include hypoxia (strongly correlated as it reflects early systemic involvement and risk of respiratory failure), age greater than 55 years, hypocalcaemia, hyperglycaemia, neutrophilia, and elevated LDH and AST. Note that the actual amylase level is not of prognostic value.

title: Acute pancreatitis – GET SMASHED mnemonic for causes
content: Gallstones, Ethanol, Trauma, Steroids, Mumps (other viruses include Coxsackie B), Autoimmune (e.g. polyarteritis nodosa) and Ascaris infection, Scorpion venom, Hypertriglyceridaemia/Hyperchylomicronaemia/Hypercalcaemia/Hypothermia, ERCP, Drugs (azathioprine, mesalazine, didanosine, bendroflumethiazide, furosemide, pentamidine, steroids, sodium valproate).

title: Acute pancreatitis – Mesalazine vs sulfasalazine risk
content: Pancreatitis is 7 times more common in patients taking mesalazine than sulfasalazine.

title: Acute liver failure – Definition
content: Rapid onset of hepatocellular dysfunction leading to a variety of systemic complications.

title: Acute liver failure – Paracetamol overdose
content: Paracetamol overdose is a common cause of acute liver failure.

title: Acute liver failure – Alcohol as cause
content: Alcohol is a cause of acute liver failure.

title: Acute liver failure – Viral hepatitis
content: Viral hepatitis (usually A or B) can cause acute liver failure.

title: Acute liver failure – Acute fatty liver of pregnancy
content: Acute fatty liver of pregnancy is a cause of acute liver failure.

title: Acute liver failure – Jaundice
content: Jaundice is a feature of acute liver failure.

title: Acute liver failure – Coagulopathy
content: Coagulopathy with raised prothrombin time occurs in acute liver failure.

title: Acute liver failure – Hypoalbuminaemia
content: Hypoalbuminaemia is a feature of acute liver failure.

title: Acute liver failure – Hepatic encephalopathy
content: Hepatic encephalopathy occurs in acute liver failure.

title: Acute liver failure – Hepatorenal syndrome
content: Renal failure is common in acute liver failure, termed hepatorenal syndrome.

title: Acute liver failure – Assessment of synthetic function
content: Liver function tests do not always accurately reflect the synthetic function of the liver. This is best assessed by looking at the prothrombin time and albumin level.

title: Upper GI bleeding – Common causes
content: Most commonly due to either oesophageal varices or peptic ulcer disease.

title: Upper GI bleeding – Haematemesis characteristics
content: The most common presenting feature. Often bright red but may sometimes be described as coffee ground.

title: Upper GI bleeding – Melaena definition
content: The passage of altered blood per rectum, typically black and tarry.

title: Upper GI bleeding – Raised urea mechanism
content: A raised urea may be seen due to the protein meal of the blood.

title: Upper GI bleeding – Glasgow-Blatchford score
content: The Glasgow-Blatchford score at first assessment helps clinicians decide whether patients can be managed as outpatients or not.

title: Upper GI bleeding – Rockall score
content: The Rockall score is used after endoscopy and provides a percentage risk of rebleeding and mortality. Includes age, features of shock, co-morbidities, aetiology of bleeding and endoscopic stigmata of recent haemorrhage.

title: Upper GI bleeding – Blatchford score zero
content: Patients with a Blatchford score of 0 may be considered for early discharge.

title: Oesophageal varices – Volume and features
content: Usually a large volume of fresh blood. Swallowed blood may cause melaena. Often associated with haemodynamic compromise. May stop spontaneously but re-bleeds are common until appropriately managed.

title: Oesophagitis – Bleeding characteristics
content: Small volume of fresh blood, often streaking vomit. Melaena rare. Often ceases spontaneously. Usually history of antecedent GORD-type symptoms.

title: Mallory-Weiss tear – Definition
content: A mucosal laceration at the gastro-oesophageal junction, usually caused by forceful retching or vomiting.

title: Mallory-Weiss tear – Typical presentation
content: Typically brisk small to moderate volume of bright red blood following a bout of repeated vomiting. Melaena is rare. Usually ceases spontaneously.

title: Mallory-Weiss tear – Preceding triggers
content: Preceding triggers may include alcohol excess, gastritis or pregnancy-related vomiting.

title: Mallory-Weiss tear – Investigation
content: An upper endoscopy is recommended to confirm the diagnosis, exclude alternative causes of upper gastrointestinal bleeding and provide endoscopic therapy if active bleeding is seen.

title: Mallory-Weiss tear – Conservative management
content: Most tears stop bleeding spontaneously and can be managed conservatively with antiemetics and proton pump inhibitors.

title: Mallory-Weiss tear – Endoscopic intervention
content: Endoscopic intervention (e.g. clipping, injection therapy or thermal coagulation) is used if ongoing or recurrent bleeding occurs.

title: Ascites – Definition
content: Accumulation of fluid in the peritoneal cavity.

title: Ascites – Prophylactic antibiotics indication
content: NICE recommend offering prophylactic oral ciprofloxacin or norfloxacin for people with cirrhosis and ascites with an ascitic protein of 15 g/litre or less, until the ascites has resolved.

title: Ascites – TIPS consideration
content: A transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt (TIPS) may be considered in some patients.

title: IBS – Diagnostic duration
content: The diagnosis of IBS should be considered if the patient has had abdominal pain, bloating, or change in bowel habit for at least 6 months.

title: IBS – Positive diagnostic criteria
content: A positive diagnosis of IBS should be made if the patient has abdominal pain relieved by defecation or associated with altered bowel frequency or stool form, in addition to 2 of the following 4 symptoms: altered stool passage (straining, urgency, incomplete evacuation), abdominal bloating, symptoms made worse by eating, passage of mucus.

title: IBS – Associated features
content: Features such as lethargy, nausea, backache and bladder symptoms may also support the diagnosis.

title: IBS – Red flag features
content: Red flag features include rectal bleeding, unexplained/unintentional weight loss, family history of bowel or ovarian cancer, and onset after 60 years of age.

title: IBS – Primary care investigations
content: Suggested primary care investigations are full blood count, ESR/CRP, and coeliac disease screen (tissue transglutaminase antibodies).

title: IBS – First-line for pain
content: For pain, cramping and bloating: antispasmodic agents (e.g. mebeverine).

title: IBS – First-line for constipation
content: For constipation: laxatives but avoid lactulose.

title: IBS – First-line for diarrhoea
content: For diarrhoea: loperamide is first-line.

title: IBS – Linaclotide indication
content: For patients with constipation who are not responding to conventional laxatives, linaclotide may be considered if optimal or maximum tolerated doses of previous laxatives from different classes have not helped and they have had constipation for at least 12 months.

title: IBS – Second-line pharmacological treatment
content: Low-dose tricyclic antidepressants (e.g. amitriptyline 5-10 mg) are used in preference to selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors.

title: IBS – Psychological interventions
content: If symptoms do not respond to pharmacological treatments after 12 months and who develop a continuing symptom profile (refractory IBS), consider referring for cognitive behavioural therapy, hypnotherapy or psychological therapy.

title: Cirrhosis – Common causes in UK
content: Alcohol, non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD), and viral hepatitis (B and C).

title: Cirrhosis – Traditional diagnosis method
content: Traditionally a liver biopsy was used. This procedure is however associated with adverse effects such as bleeding and pain.

title: Cirrhosis – Transient elastography
content: Transient elastography (brand name Fibroscan) uses a 50-MHz wave passed into the liver from a small transducer on the end of an ultrasound probe. Measures the stiffness of the liver which is a proxy for fibrosis.

title: Cirrhosis – NICE screening recommendations
content: NICE recommend offering transient elastography to people with hepatitis C virus infection, men who drink over 50 units of alcohol per week and women who drink over 35 units of alcohol per week and have done so for several months, and people diagnosed with alcohol-related liver disease.

title: Cirrhosis – Upper endoscopy for varices
content: NICE recommend doing an upper endoscopy to check for varices in patients with a new diagnosis of cirrhosis.

title: Cirrhosis – Hepatocellular cancer surveillance
content: Liver ultrasound every 6 months (+/- alpha-fetoprotein) to check for hepatocellular cancer.

title: Malnutrition – NICE definition criteria 1
content: A Body Mass Index (BMI) of less than 18.5.

title: Malnutrition – NICE definition criteria 2
content: Unintentional weight loss greater than 10% within the last 3-6 months.

title: Malnutrition – NICE definition criteria 3
content: A BMI of less than 20 and unintentional weight loss greater than 5% within the last 3-6 months.

title: Malnutrition – Prevalence in elderly
content: Around 10% of patients aged over 65 years are malnourished, the vast majority of those living independently.

title: Malnutrition – MUST screening tool
content: Screening for malnutrition is mostly done using MUST (Malnutrition Universal Screen Tool). It should be done on admission to care/nursing homes and hospital, or if there is a concern. It takes into account BMI, recent weight change and the presence of acute disease.

title: Coeliac disease – Definition
content: An autoimmune condition caused by sensitivity to the protein gluten.

title: Coeliac disease – Prevalence
content: Thought to affect around 1% of the UK population.

title: Coeliac disease – Pathophysiology
content: Repeated exposure to gluten leads to villous atrophy which in turn causes malabsorption.

title: Coeliac disease – HLA associations
content: Strongly associated with HLA-DQ2 (95% of patients) and HLA-DQ8 (80%).

title: Coeliac disease – Associated conditions
content: Conditions associated with coeliac disease include dermatitis herpetiformis (a vesicular, pruritic skin eruption) and autoimmune disorders (type 1 diabetes mellitus and autoimmune hepatitis).

title: Coeliac disease – Screening indications symptoms
content: NICE suggest screening patients with chronic or intermittent diarrhoea, failure to thrive or faltering growth (in children), persistent or unexplained gastrointestinal symptoms including nausea and vomiting, prolonged fatigue, recurrent abdominal pain cramping or distension, sudden or unexpected weight loss, and unexplained iron-deficiency anaemia or other unspecified anaemia.

title: Coeliac disease – Screening indications conditions
content: NICE suggest screening patients with autoimmune thyroid disease, dermatitis herpetiformis, irritable bowel syndrome, type 1 diabetes, and first-degree relatives with coeliac disease.

title: Coeliac disease – Anaemia complications
content: Anaemia due to iron, folate and vitamin B12 deficiency. Folate deficiency is more common than vitamin B12 deficiency in coeliac disease.

title: Coeliac disease – Hyposplenism
content: Hyposplenism is a complication of coeliac disease.

title: Coeliac disease – Bone complications
content: Osteoporosis and osteomalacia are complications.

title: Coeliac disease – Lactose intolerance
content: Lactose intolerance is a complication.

title: Coeliac disease – T-cell lymphoma
content: Enteropathy-associated T-cell lymphoma of small intestine is a complication.

title: Coeliac disease – Reproductive complications
content: Subfertility and unfavourable pregnancy outcomes are complications.

title: Coeliac disease – Malignancy risk
content: Rare complications include oesophageal cancer and other malignancies.

title: Coeliac disease – First-choice serology
content: Tissue transglutaminase (TTG) antibodies (IgA) are first-choice according to NICE.

title: Coeliac disease – Endomyseal antibody
content: Endomyseal antibody (IgA) is used in diagnosis.

title: Coeliac disease – IgA deficiency testing
content: Need to look for selective IgA deficiency, which would give a false negative coeliac result. If IgA deficiency, test for IgG endomyseal antibodies, IgG deamidated gliadin peptide (DGP) or IgG transglutaminase antibodies.

title: Coeliac disease – Anti-gliadin antibody
content: Anti-gliadin antibody (IgA or IgG) tests are not recommended by NICE.

title: Coeliac disease – Gluten reintroduction before testing
content: If patients are already taking a gluten-free diet they should be asked, if possible, to reintroduce gluten for at least 6 weeks prior to testing.

title: Coeliac disease – Endoscopic biopsy gold standard
content: Endoscopic intestinal biopsy is the gold standard for diagnosis and should be performed in all patients with suspected coeliac disease to confirm or exclude the diagnosis. Traditionally done in the duodenum but jejunal biopsies are also sometimes performed.

title: Coeliac disease – Biopsy findings
content: Findings supportive of coeliac disease include villous atrophy, crypt hyperplasia, increase in intraepithelial lymphocytes, and lamina propria infiltration with lymphocytes.

title: Coeliac disease – Gluten-containing cereals
content: Gluten-containing cereals include wheat (bread, pasta, pastry), barley (beer), rye, and oats (though some patients with coeliac disease appear able to tolerate oats).

title: Coeliac disease – Whisky safety
content: Whisky is made using malted barley. Proteins such as gluten are however removed during the distillation process making it safe to drink for patients with coeliac disease.

title: Coeliac disease – Gluten-free foods
content: Notable foods which are gluten-free include rice, potatoes, and corn (maize).

title: Coeliac disease – Monitoring compliance
content: Tissue transglutaminase antibodies may be checked to check compliance with a gluten-free diet.

title: Coeliac disease – Pneumococcal vaccination
content: Patients with coeliac disease often have a degree of functional hyposplenism. For this reason, all patients with coeliac disease are offered the pneumococcal vaccine. Coeliac UK recommends that everyone with coeliac disease is vaccinated against pneumococcal infection and has a booster every 5 years.

title: Coeliac disease – Influenza vaccination
content: Current guidelines suggest giving the influenza vaccine on an individual basis.

title: C. difficile – Definition
content: A Gram positive rod that produces an exotoxin which causes intestinal damage leading to pseudomembranous colitis.

title: C. difficile – Pathophysiology mechanism
content: Develops when the normal gut flora are suppressed by broad-spectrum antibiotics. Anaerobic gram-positive, spore-forming, toxin-producing bacillus. Transmission via the faecal-oral route by ingestion of spores. Releases two exotoxins (toxin A and toxin B) that act on intestinal epithelial cells and inflammatory cells resulting in colitis.

title: C. difficile – Leading antibiotic cause
content: Second and third-generation cephalosporins are now the leading cause of C. difficile. Clindamycin is historically associated.

title: C. difficile – Proton pump inhibitors as risk factor
content: Proton pump inhibitors are a risk factor.

title: C. difficile – Clinical features
content: Diarrhoea, abdominal pain, and a raised white blood cell count (WCC) is characteristic. If severe, toxic megacolon may develop.

title: C. difficile – Severity scale mild
content: Mild: Normal WCC.

title: C. difficile – Severity scale moderate
content: Moderate: Increased WCC (less than 15 x 10^9/L), typically 3-5 loose stools per day.

title: C. difficile – Severity scale severe
content: Severe: Increased WCC (greater than 15 x 10^9/L) or an acutely increased creatinine (greater than 50% above baseline) or a temperature greater than 38.5°C or evidence of severe colitis (abdominal or radiological signs).

title: C. difficile – Severity scale life-threatening
content: Life-threatening: Hypotension, partial or complete ileus, toxic megacolon, or CT evidence of severe disease.

title: C. difficile – Diagnosis method
content: Diagnosis is made by detecting C. difficile toxin (CDT) in the stool. C. difficile antigen positivity only shows exposure to the bacteria, rather than current infection.

title: C. difficile – First episode first-line treatment
content: Oral vancomycin for 10 days.

title: C. difficile – First episode second-line treatment
content: Oral fidaxomicin.

title: C. difficile – First episode third-line treatment
content: Oral vancomycin +/- IV metronidazole.

title: C. difficile – Recurrence rate
content: Recurrent infection occurs in around 20% of patients, increasing to 50% after their second episode.

title: C. difficile – Recurrence within 12 weeks
content: Within 12 weeks of symptom resolution: oral fidaxomicin.

title: C. difficile – Recurrence after 12 weeks
content: After 12 weeks of symptom resolution: oral vancomycin OR fidaxomicin.

title: C. difficile – Life-threatening treatment
content: Oral vancomycin AND IV metronidazole.

title: C. difficile – Bezlotoxumab
content: A monoclonal antibody which targets C. difficile toxin B. NICE do not currently support its use to prevent recurrences as it is not cost-effective.

title: C. difficile – Faecal microbiota transplant
content: May be considered for patients who have had 2 or more previous episodes.

title: C. difficile – Isolation requirements
content: Isolation in side room: the patient should remain isolated until there has been no diarrhoea (types 5-7 on the Bristol Stool Chart) for at least 48 hours.

title: C. difficile – Hand hygiene
content: Hand washing is essential - alcohol gel does not kill the spores of C. difficile.

title: Crohn's disease – Definition
content: A form of inflammatory bowel disease that commonly affects the terminal ileum and colon but may be seen anywhere from the mouth to anus.

title: Crohn's disease – Genetic susceptibility
content: The cause is unknown but there is a strong genetic susceptibility.

title: Crohn's disease – Transmural inflammation
content: Inflammation occurs in all layers, down to the serosa. This is why patients with Crohn's are prone to strictures, fistulas and adhesions.

title: Crohn's disease – Distribution pattern
content: 80% of patients have small bowel involvement, usually in the ileum, with around 30% of patients having ileitis exclusively. 50% of patients have ileocolitis. 20% of patients have colitis exclusively. 30% of patients have perianal disease.

title: Crohn's disease – Age of presentation
content: Typically presents in late adolescence or early adulthood.

title: Crohn's disease – Non-specific symptoms
content: Presentation may be non-specific symptoms such as weight loss and lethargy.

title: Crohn's disease – Diarrhoea in adults
content: Diarrhoea is the most prominent symptom in adults. Crohn's colitis may cause bloody diarrhoea.

title: Crohn's disease – Abdominal pain in children
content: Abdominal pain is the most prominent symptom in children.

title: Crohn's disease – Perianal disease
content: Perianal disease includes skin tags or ulcers.

title: Crohn's disease – Extra-intestinal features prevalence
content: Extra-intestinal features are more common in patients with colitis or perianal disease.

title: Crohn's disease – Laboratory findings
content: Raised inflammatory markers, increased faecal calprotectin, anaemia, low vitamin B12 and vitamin D.

title: Crohn's disease – CRP correlation
content: C-reactive protein correlates well with disease activity.

title: Crohn's disease – Investigation of choice
content: Colonoscopy is the investigation of choice. Features suggestive of Crohn's include deep ulcers and skip lesions.

title: Crohn's disease – Histological features
content: Inflammation in all layers from mucosa to serosa, goblet cells, and granulomas.

title: Crohn's disease – Small bowel enema findings
content: High sensitivity and specificity for examination of the terminal ileum. Findings include strictures (Kantor's string sign), proximal bowel dilation, rose thorn ulcers, and fistulae.

title: Crohn's disease – Smoking cessation importance
content: Patients should be strongly advised to stop smoking. Smoking makes Crohn's worse.

title: Crohn's disease – NSAIDs and COCP
content: Some studies suggest an increased risk of relapse secondary to NSAIDs and the combined oral contraceptive pill but the evidence is patchy.

title: Crohn's disease – Inducing remission with glucocorticoids
content: Glucocorticoids (oral, topical or intravenous) are generally used to induce remission. Budesonide is an alternative in a subgroup of patients.

title: Crohn's disease – Enteral feeding
content: Enteral feeding with an elemental diet may be used in addition to or instead of other measures to induce remission, particularly if there is concern regarding the side-effects of steroids (for example in young children).

title: Crohn's disease – 5-ASA drugs
content: 5-ASA drugs (e.g. mesalazine) are used second-line to glucocorticoids but are not as effective.

title: Crohn's disease – Azathioprine as add-on
content: Azathioprine or mercaptopurine may be used as an add-on medication to induce remission but is not used as monotherapy. Methotrexate is an alternative to azathioprine.

title: Crohn's disease – Infliximab indication
content: Infliximab is useful in refractory disease and fistulating Crohn's. Patients typically continue on azathioprine or methotrexate.

title: Crohn's disease – Metronidazole for perianal disease
content: Metronidazole is often used for isolated peri-anal disease.

title: Crohn's disease – Maintaining remission first-line
content: Azathioprine or mercaptopurine is used first-line to maintain remission. TPMT activity should be assessed before starting.

title: Crohn's disease – Maintaining remission second-line
content: Methotrexate is used second-line.

title: Crohn's disease – Surgical rate
content: Around 80% of patients with Crohn's disease will eventually have surgery.

title: Crohn's disease – Ileocaecal resection
content: Stricturing terminal ileal disease is treated with ileocaecal resection.

title: Crohn's disease – Perianal fistulae investigation
content: MRI is the investigation of choice for suspected perianal fistulae - can be used to determine if there is an abscess and if the fistula is simple (low fistula) or complex (high fistula that passes through or above muscle layers).

title: Crohn's disease – Perianal fistulae medical management
content: Patients with symptomatic perianal fistulae are usually given oral metronidazole. Anti-TNF agents such as infliximab may also be effective in closing and maintaining closure of perianal fistulas.

title: Crohn's disease – Draining seton
content: A draining seton is used for complex fistulae. A seton is a piece of surgical thread that's left in the fistula for several weeks to keep it open.

title: Crohn's disease – Perianal abscess management
content: Requires incision and drainage combined with antibiotic therapy. A draining seton may also be placed if a tract is identified.

title: Crohn's disease – Small bowel cancer risk
content: Small bowel cancer (standard incidence ratio = 40).

title: Crohn's disease – Colorectal cancer risk
content: Colorectal cancer (standard incidence ratio = 2, i.e. less than the risk associated with ulcerative colitis).

title: Crohn's disease – Osteoporosis complication
content: Osteoporosis is a complication.

title: IBD – Arthritis related to activity
content: Pauciarticular, asymmetric arthritis related to disease activity. Arthritis is the most common extra-intestinal feature in both Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis.

title: IBD – Erythema nodosum
content: Erythema nodosum related to disease activity.

title: IBD – Episcleritis
content: Episcleritis related to disease activity. More common in Crohn's disease.

title: IBD – Osteoporosis
content: Osteoporosis is common to both Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis.

title: IBD – Arthritis unrelated to activity
content: Polyarticular, symmetric arthritis unrelated to disease activity.

title: IBD – Uveitis
content: Uveitis unrelated to disease activity. More common in ulcerative colitis.

title: IBD – Pyoderma gangrenosum
content: Pyoderma gangrenosum unrelated to disease activity.

title: IBD – Clubbing
content: Clubbing unrelated to disease activity.

title: IBD – Primary sclerosing cholangitis
content: Primary sclerosing cholangitis unrelated to disease activity. Much more common in ulcerative colitis.

title: Constipation – Definition
content: Infrequent bowel movements or difficulty passing stools.

title: Diarrhoea – WHO definition
content: Greater than 3 loose or watery stools per day.

title: Diarrhoea – Acute definition
content: Acute diarrhoea is less than 14 days.

title: Diarrhoea – Chronic definition
content: Chronic diarrhoea is greater than 14 days.

title: Ulcerative colitis – Definition
content: Inflammatory bowel disease affecting the colon and rectum with continuous inflammation.

title: Ulcerative colitis – Distribution
content: Inflammation always starts at the rectum and never spreads beyond the ileocaecal valve.

title: Ulcerative colitis – Bloody diarrhoea
content: Bloody diarrhoea is the primary symptom.

title: Ulcerative colitis – Severity mild
content: Mild: less than 4 stools per day, only a small amount of blood.

title: Ulcerative colitis – Severity moderate
content: Moderate: 4-6 stools per day, varying amounts of blood, no systemic upset.

title: Ulcerative colitis – Severity severe
content: Severe: greater than 6 bloody stools per day plus features of systemic upset (pyrexia, tachycardia, anaemia, raised inflammatory markers).

title: Ulcerative colitis – Proctitis treatment
content: Topical (rectal) aminosalicylate. For distal colitis rectal mesalazine has been shown to be superior to rectal steroids and oral aminosalicylates.

title: Ulcerative colitis – Severe colitis treatment
content: Should be treated in hospital. IV steroids are usually given first-line. IV ciclosporin may be used if steroids are contraindicated.

title: Ulcerative colitis – 72-hour rule
content: If after 72 hours there has been no improvement, consider adding IV ciclosporin to IV corticosteroids or consider surgery.

title: Ulcerative colitis – Maintaining remission
content: Following a severe relapse or 2 or more exacerbations in the past year: oral azathioprine or oral mercaptopurine.

title: Ulcerative colitis – Methotrexate not recommended
content: Methotrexate is not recommended for the management of UC (in contrast to Crohn's disease).

title: Ulcerative colitis – Surgical indications
content: Surgery is considered when UC is unresponsive to optimal medical therapy or in the presence of serious complications such as toxic megacolon or perforation.

title: Ulcerative colitis – Restorative proctocolectomy
content: The preferred surgical approach involves total colectomy with the formation of an ileal pouch joined to the anal canal (IPAA). A temporary loop ileostomy is created and later reversed.

title: GORD – Definition
content: Gastro-oesophageal reflux disease characterized by reflux of gastric contents into the oesophagus.

title: GORD – Heartburn
content: Burning retrosternal sensation.

title: GORD – Acid regurgitation
content: Acid regurgitation into the mouth.

title: GORD – Dysphagia
content: Dysphagia may occur.

title: GORD – PPI first-line
content: Proton pump inhibitors are first-line treatment.

title: GORD – Barrett's oesophagus
content: Barrett's oesophagus is a complication where squamous epithelium is replaced by columnar epithelium, increasing cancer risk.

title: Peptic ulcer disease – Definition
content: Ulceration of the stomach or duodenum.

title: Peptic ulcer disease – H. pylori association
content: Helicobacter pylori is the most common cause.

title: Peptic ulcer disease – NSAIDs as cause
content: NSAIDs are a major cause of peptic ulcers.

title: Peptic ulcer disease – Epigastric pain
content: Epigastric pain is the main symptom.

title: Peptic ulcer disease – Duodenal ulcer pain timing
content: Duodenal ulcer pain is typically relieved by eating.

title: Peptic ulcer disease – Gastric ulcer pain timing
content: Gastric ulcer pain is typically worsened by eating.

title: Peptic ulcer disease – Endoscopy diagnosis
content: Upper GI endoscopy is the gold standard for diagnosis.

title: Peptic ulcer disease – H. pylori eradication
content: Triple therapy: PPI plus two antibiotics (amoxicillin and clarithromycin or metronidazole) for 7 days.

title: Peptic ulcer disease – Perforation complication
content: Perforation is a serious complication.

title: Peptic ulcer disease – Bleeding complication
content: Upper GI bleeding is a complication.

title: Diverticular disease – Definition
content: Outpouchings of the colonic mucosa through the muscular wall.

title: Diverticular disease – Common location
content: Most commonly affects the sigmoid colon.

title: Diverticular disease – Asymptomatic diverticulosis
content: Most patients with diverticulosis are asymptomatic.

title: Diverticulitis – Definition
content: Inflammation of diverticula.

title: Diverticulitis – Left lower quadrant pain
content: Classically causes left lower quadrant pain.

title: Diverticulitis – Fever
content: Fever is common in diverticulitis.

title: Diverticulitis – Change in bowel habit
content: May cause diarrhoea or constipation.

title: Diverticulitis – CT diagnosis
content: CT abdomen is the investigation of choice.

title: Diverticulitis – Antibiotic treatment
content: Antibiotics are first-line for uncomplicated diverticulitis.

title: Diverticulitis – Perforation complication
content: Perforation may occur requiring surgery.

title: Diverticulitis – Fistula formation
content: Fistulae may form, commonly colovesical.

title: Gallstones – Definition
content: Stones formed in the gallbladder.

title: Gallstones – Risk factors 4Fs
content: Female, Fat, Fertile, Forty.

title: Gallstones – Asymptomatic
content: Most gallstones are asymptomatic.

title: Biliary colic – Definition
content: Pain caused by gallstone temporarily obstructing the cystic duct.

title: Biliary colic – Pain characteristics
content: Severe right upper quadrant pain, often after fatty meals, lasting 30 minutes to several hours.

title: Biliary colic – Normal LFTs
content: Liver function tests are typically normal in uncomplicated biliary colic.

title: Biliary colic – Ultrasound diagnosis
content: Ultrasound is the first-line investigation.

title: Biliary colic – Elective cholecystectomy
content: Elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy is the definitive treatment.

title: Acute cholangitis – Definition
content: Infection of the bile duct, usually due to obstruction.

title: Acute cholangitis – Charcot's triad
content: Fever, right upper quadrant pain, and jaundice.

title: Acute cholangitis – Reynolds' pentad
content: Charcot's triad plus hypotension and confusion.

title: Acute cholangitis – Raised ALP
content: Obstructive pattern of LFTs with raised alkaline phosphatase and bilirubin.

title: Acute cholangitis – ERCP treatment
content: ERCP with sphincterotomy and stone extraction is the treatment of choice.

title: Acute cholangitis – Antibiotics
content: Broad-spectrum IV antibiotics are essential.

title: Haemochromatosis – Definition
content: Inherited disorder of iron metabolism leading to iron overload.

title: Haemochromatosis – HFE gene mutation
content: Caused by mutations in the HFE gene, most commonly C282Y.

title: Haemochromatosis – Bronze diabetes
content: Classical triad: bronze skin pigmentation, diabetes mellitus, and cirrhosis.

title: Haemochromatosis – Arthropathy
content: Arthropathy affecting small joints of the hands.

title: Haemochromatosis – Cardiomyopathy
content: Dilated cardiomyopathy may occur.

title: Haemochromatosis – Raised ferritin
content: Raised serum ferritin and transferrin saturation.

title: Haemochromatosis – Genetic testing
content: HFE gene testing confirms diagnosis.

title: Haemochromatosis – Venesection treatment
content: Regular venesection is the mainstay of treatment.

title: Hepatitis – Definition
content: Inflammation of the liver.

title: Hepatitis A – Transmission
content: Faecal-oral transmission.

title: Hepatitis A – Self-limiting
content: Usually self-limiting acute infection.

title: Hepatitis B – Transmission
content: Blood-borne and sexual transmission.

title: Hepatitis B – Chronic infection
content: Can lead to chronic infection, cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma.

title: Hepatitis B – Surface antigen
content: HBsAg positive indicates active infection.

title: Hepatitis B – Vaccination
content: Effective vaccination available.

title: Hepatitis C – Transmission
content: Primarily blood-borne transmission.

title: Hepatitis C – Chronic infection rate
content: Around 80% develop chronic infection.

title: Hepatitis C – Direct-acting antivirals
content: Treated with direct-acting antivirals with high cure rates.

title: Autoimmune hepatitis – Definition
content: Chronic hepatitis of unknown cause with autoimmune features.

title: Autoimmune hepatitis – Female predominance
content: More common in young and middle-aged women.

title: Autoimmune hepatitis – ANA and SMA
content: Associated with positive ANA and anti-smooth muscle antibodies.

title: Autoimmune hepatitis – Steroid treatment
content: Treated with corticosteroids and azathioprine.

title: Gastric cancer – Definition
content: Malignant tumor of the stomach.

title: Gastric cancer – H. pylori risk
content: Helicobacter pylori infection is a major risk factor.

title: Gastric cancer – Weight loss
content: Weight loss and anorexia are common.

title: Gastric cancer – Dyspepsia
content: Persistent dyspepsia in older patients.

title: Gastric cancer – Vomiting
content: Vomiting may occur, especially with gastric outlet obstruction.

title: Gastric cancer – Upper GI bleeding
content: May present with upper GI bleeding.

title: Gastric cancer – Endoscopy diagnosis
content: Upper GI endoscopy with biopsy is diagnostic.

title: Gastric cancer – Surgical resection
content: Surgical resection offers the only chance of cure.

title: Oesophageal cancer – Types
content: Squamous cell carcinoma and adenocarcinoma.

title: Oesophageal cancer – Adenocarcinoma association
content: Adenocarcinoma associated with Barrett's oesophagus and GORD.

title: Oesophageal cancer – Squamous risk factors
content: Squamous cell carcinoma associated with smoking and alcohol.

title: Oesophageal cancer – Progressive dysphagia
content: Progressive dysphagia is the main symptom.

title: Oesophageal cancer – Weight loss
content: Weight loss is common.

title: Oesophageal cancer – Endoscopy and biopsy
content: Upper GI endoscopy with biopsy is diagnostic.

title: Oesophageal cancer – Staging CT
content: CT chest, abdomen and pelvis for staging.

title: Oesophageal cancer – Oesophagectomy
content: Oesophagectomy with chemotherapy or chemoradiotherapy.

title: Pancreatic cancer – Definition
content: Malignant tumor of the pancreas, usually adenocarcinoma.

title: Pancreatic cancer – Poor prognosis
content: Very poor prognosis with low 5-year survival.

title: Pancreatic cancer – Painless jaundice
content: Painless jaundice if tumor in head of pancreas.

title: Pancreatic cancer – Epigastric pain
content: Epigastric pain radiating to back.

title: Pancreatic cancer – Weight loss
content: Significant weight loss.

title: Pancreatic cancer – CA 19-9
content: CA 19-9 tumor marker may be raised.

title: Pancreatic cancer – CT diagnosis
content: CT pancreas is the main diagnostic investigation.

title: Pancreatic cancer – Whipple procedure
content: Whipple procedure (pancreaticoduodenectomy) for resectable tumors.

title: Colorectal cancer – Definition
content: Malignant tumor of the colon or rectum.

title: Colorectal cancer – Change in bowel habit
content: Change in bowel habit is a key symptom.

title: Colorectal cancer – Rectal bleeding
content: Rectal bleeding, especially in older patients.

title: Colorectal cancer – Iron deficiency anaemia
content: May present with iron deficiency anaemia.

title: Colorectal cancer – Colonoscopy diagnosis
content: Colonoscopy with biopsy is diagnostic.

title: Colorectal cancer – CEA marker
content: CEA (carcinoembryonic antigen) may be raised.

title: Colorectal cancer – Surgical resection
content: Surgical resection is the main treatment.

title: Colorectal cancer – Adjuvant chemotherapy
content: Adjuvant chemotherapy for advanced disease.

title: Haemorrhoids – Definition
content: Swollen vascular cushions in the anal canal.

title: Haemorrhoids – Internal vs external
content: Internal haemorrhoids above the dentate line, external below.

title: Haemorrhoids – Painless bleeding
content: Bright red painless rectal bleeding.

title: Haemorrhoids – Prolapse
content: May prolapse through the anus.

title: Haemorrhoids – Conservative management
content: Increase dietary fiber and fluid intake.

title: Haemorrhoids – Rubber band ligation
content: Rubber band ligation for internal haemorrhoids.

title: Haemorrhoids – Haemorrhoidectomy
content: Surgical haemorrhoidectomy for severe cases.

title: Anal fissure – Definition
content: Tear in the lining of the anal canal.

title: Anal fissure – Painful defecation
content: Severe pain during and after defecation.

title: Anal fissure – Bright red bleeding
content: Small amount of bright red blood on toilet paper.

title: Anal fissure – Posterior midline
content: Most commonly occurs in the posterior midline.

title: Anal fissure – GTN ointment
content: Topical glyceryl trinitrate (GTN) ointment first-line.

title: Anal fissure – Botulinum toxin
content: Botulinum toxin injection for chronic fissures.

title: Anal fissure – Lateral sphincterotomy
content: Lateral internal sphincterotomy for refractory cases.

title: Hernias – Definition
content: Protrusion of an organ or tissue through an abnormal opening.

title: Inguinal hernia – Most common
content: Most common type of hernia.

title: Inguinal hernia – Direct vs indirect
content: Direct hernias protrude through Hesselbach's triangle. Indirect hernias pass through the internal inguinal ring.

title: Inguinal hernia – Reducible
content: Reducible hernias can be pushed back.

title: Inguinal hernia – Incarceration
content: Incarcerated hernias cannot be reduced.

title: Inguinal hernia – Strangulation
content: Strangulated hernias have compromised blood supply, causing severe pain and requiring emergency surgery.

title: Inguinal hernia – Surgical repair
content: Surgical repair with mesh is the definitive treatment.

title: Femoral hernia – Female predominance
content: More common in women.

title: Femoral hernia – High strangulation risk
content: Higher risk of strangulation than inguinal hernias.

title: Umbilical hernia – Congenital
content: Common in infants, often resolve spontaneously.

title: Incisional hernia – Post-surgical
content: Occurs at the site of previous surgical incision.

title: Hiatus hernia – Definition
content: Herniation of the stomach through the diaphragmatic hiatus.

title: Hiatus hernia – Sliding type
content: Sliding hiatus hernia: gastro-oesophageal junction moves above the diaphragm. Most common type.

title: Hiatus hernia – Rolling type
content: Rolling (para-oesophageal) hiatus hernia: gastro-oesophageal junction remains below diaphragm but part of stomach herniates.

title: Hiatus hernia – GORD symptoms
content: Often asymptomatic or associated with GORD symptoms.

title: Hiatus hernia – Barium swallow
content: Diagnosed on barium swallow or endoscopy.

title: Hiatus hernia – PPI treatment
content: Managed with PPIs for reflux symptoms.

title: Hiatus hernia – Surgical repair
content: Fundoplication surgery for severe cases.

title: Alcoholic hepatitis – Definition
content: Acute inflammation of the liver due to alcohol consumption.

title: Alcoholic hepatitis – Spectrum of disease
content: Part of the spectrum of alcoholic liver disease, which includes fatty liver, alcoholic hepatitis, and cirrhosis.

title: Alcoholic hepatitis – Jaundice
content: Jaundice is a key feature.

title: Alcoholic hepatitis – Hepatomegaly
content: Tender hepatomegaly may be present.

title: Alcoholic hepatitis – Fever
content: Fever is common.

title: Alcoholic hepatitis – Raised AST and ALT
content: AST is typically higher than ALT (AST:ALT ratio greater than 2:1).

title: Alcoholic hepatitis – Maddrey discriminant function
content: Maddrey discriminant function is used to assess severity and guide treatment.

title: Alcoholic hepatitis – Corticosteroids
content: Corticosteroids (prednisolone) for severe cases with Maddrey score greater than or equal to 32.

title: Alcoholic hepatitis – Abstinence
content: Alcohol abstinence is essential.

title: Alcoholic hepatitis – Nutritional support
content: Nutritional support is important as patients are often malnourished.

title: Anaemia – Definition
content: Reduced haemoglobin concentration below normal range.

title: Anaemia – Iron deficiency in GI disease
content: Iron deficiency anaemia is common in GI bleeding, coeliac disease, and inflammatory bowel disease.

title: Anaemia – B12 deficiency causes
content: Vitamin B12 deficiency may occur in pernicious anaemia, terminal ileal disease (Crohn's), or post-gastrectomy.

title: Anaemia – Folate deficiency causes
content: Folate deficiency may occur in coeliac disease, alcohol excess, or dietary insufficiency.

title: Anaemia – Chronic disease anaemia
content: Anaemia of chronic disease is normochromic normocytic and occurs in chronic inflammatory conditions like IBD.

title: Eating disorders – Definition
content: Psychological disorders characterized by abnormal eating habits.

title: Eating disorders – Anorexia nervosa
content: Anorexia nervosa involves restriction of energy intake leading to significantly low body weight.

title: Eating disorders – Bulimia nervosa
content: Bulimia nervosa involves recurrent episodes of binge eating followed by compensatory behaviors.

title: Eating disorders – GI complications
content: GI complications include delayed gastric emptying, constipation, and refeeding syndrome.

title: GI perforation – Definition
content: Full-thickness breach of the gastrointestinal tract wall.

title: GI perforation – Causes
content: Causes include peptic ulcer disease, diverticulitis, appendicitis, trauma, and iatrogenic (endoscopy).

title: GI perforation – Sudden severe pain
content: Sudden onset severe abdominal pain.

title: GI perforation – Peritonitis signs
content: Signs of peritonitis: rigid abdomen, guarding, rebound tenderness.

title: GI perforation – Free air on imaging
content: Free air under the diaphragm on erect chest X-ray or CT.

title: GI perforation – Emergency surgery
content: Emergency laparotomy or laparoscopy is required.

title: GI perforation – Broad-spectrum antibiotics
content: Broad-spectrum IV antibiotics are essential.

title: Hyposplenism – Definition
content: Reduced splenic function.

title: Hyposplenism – Causes
content: Causes include coeliac disease, sickle cell disease, inflammatory bowel disease, and splenectomy.

title: Hyposplenism – Infection risk
content: Increased risk of infection with encapsulated organisms (Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, Neisseria meningitidis).

title: Hyposplenism – Howell-Jolly bodies
content: Blood film shows Howell-Jolly bodies, target cells, and acanthocytes.

title: Hyposplenism – Vaccination
content: Vaccination against pneumococcus, Haemophilus influenzae type b, and meningococcus is essential.

title: Hyposplenism – Prophylactic antibiotics
content: Lifelong prophylactic penicillin V (or erythromycin if penicillin allergic) is recommended.

title: Infectious mononucleosis – Definition
content: Acute viral infection caused by Epstein-Barr virus (EBV).

title: Infectious mononucleosis – Triad
content: Classic triad: fever, pharyngitis, and lymphadenopathy.

title: Infectious mononucleosis – Splenomegaly
content: Splenomegaly occurs in about 50% of cases.

title: Infectious mononucleosis – Hepatomegaly
content: Hepatomegaly and deranged LFTs may occur.

title: Infectious mononucleosis – Atypical lymphocytes
content: Blood film shows atypical lymphocytes.

title: Infectious mononucleosis – Monospot test
content: Monospot test (heterophile antibody test) is positive.

title: Infectious mononucleosis – Self-limiting
content: Usually self-limiting, supportive management.

title: Infectious mononucleosis – Avoid contact sports
content: Avoid contact sports for 4-6 weeks due to risk of splenic rupture.

title: Malabsorption – Definition
content: Impaired absorption of nutrients from the gastrointestinal tract.

title: Malabsorption – Causes
content: Causes include coeliac disease, Crohn's disease, chronic pancreatitis, bacterial overgrowth, and lactose intolerance.

title: Malabsorption – Chronic diarrhoea
content: Chronic diarrhoea, often steatorrhoea (fatty, pale, bulky stools).

title: Malabsorption – Weight loss
content: Weight loss despite adequate dietary intake.

title: Malabsorption – Nutritional deficiencies
content: Nutritional deficiencies: iron, B12, folate, fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K).

title: Malabsorption – Faecal elastase
content: Faecal elastase is low in pancreatic insufficiency.

title: Malabsorption – Treat underlying cause
content: Treatment involves addressing the underlying cause and nutritional supplementation.

title: Mesenteric adenitis – Definition
content: Inflammation of mesenteric lymph nodes, usually viral.

title: Mesenteric adenitis – Mimics appendicitis
content: Often mimics appendicitis with right lower quadrant pain.

title: Mesenteric adenitis – Preceding URTI
content: Often follows an upper respiratory tract infection.

title: Mesenteric adenitis – More common in children
content: More common in children and adolescents.

title: Mesenteric adenitis – Self-limiting
content: Usually self-limiting, supportive management.

title: Necrotising enterocolitis – Definition
content: Life-threatening condition affecting premature neonates, characterized by intestinal necrosis.

title: Necrotising enterocolitis – Premature infants
content: Primarily affects premature infants, especially those with very low birth weight.

title: Necrotising enterocolitis – Feeding intolerance
content: Feeding intolerance, abdominal distension, and bloody stools.

title: Necrotising enterocolitis – Pneumatosis intestinalis
content: Abdominal X-ray shows pneumatosis intestinalis (gas in bowel wall).

title: Necrotising enterocolitis – NBM and antibiotics
content: Nil by mouth, nasogastric decompression, IV fluids, and broad-spectrum antibiotics.

title: Necrotising enterocolitis – Surgery for perforation
content: Surgery if perforation or clinical deterioration.

title: Perianal abscess – Definition
content: Collection of pus in the perianal region.

title: Perianal abscess – Severe pain
content: Severe perianal pain, swelling, and fever.

title: Perianal abscess – Incision and drainage
content: Treatment is incision and drainage.

title: Perianal fistula – Definition
content: Abnormal tract between the anal canal and perianal skin.

title: Perianal fistula – Discharge
content: Persistent discharge from perianal opening.

title: Perianal fistula – Associated with Crohn's
content: Commonly associated with Crohn's disease.

title: Perianal fistula – MRI investigation
content: MRI is the investigation of choice.

title: Perianal fistula – Seton placement
content: Treatment may involve seton placement or fistulotomy.

title: Peritonitis – Definition
content: Inflammation of the peritoneum.

title: Peritonitis – Primary vs secondary
content: Primary (spontaneous bacterial peritonitis) occurs without obvious source. Secondary peritonitis follows perforation or surgery.

title: Peritonitis – SBP in cirrhosis
content: Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis occurs in patients with cirrhosis and ascites.

title: Peritonitis – Abdominal pain and rigidity
content: Severe abdominal pain with guarding and rigidity.

title: Peritonitis – Ascitic tap
content: Ascitic tap shows neutrophil count greater than 250 cells/mm³ in SBP.

title: Peritonitis – Antibiotics for SBP
content: IV cefotaxime for spontaneous bacterial peritonitis.

title: Peritonitis – Surgery for secondary
content: Secondary peritonitis requires emergency surgery to address the source.

title: B12/folate deficiency – Definition
content: Deficiency of vitamin B12 and/or folate leading to macrocytic anaemia.

title: B12 deficiency – Causes
content: Causes include pernicious anaemia, terminal ileal disease or resection, dietary insufficiency (vegans), and gastrectomy.

title: Folate deficiency – Causes
content: Causes include dietary insufficiency, coeliac disease, alcohol excess, and certain medications (methotrexate).

title: B12 deficiency – Neurological features
content: B12 deficiency causes subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord: peripheral neuropathy, ataxia, and cognitive impairment.

title: B12/folate deficiency – Macrocytic anaemia
content: Macrocytic anaemia with hypersegmented neutrophils on blood film.

title: B12 deficiency – Intrinsic factor antibodies
content: Intrinsic factor antibodies are specific for pernicious anaemia.

title: B12 deficiency – IM replacement
content: Intramuscular hydroxocobalamin replacement.

title: Folate deficiency – Oral supplementation
content: Oral folic acid supplementation.

title: B12/folate – Replace B12 first
content: Always replace B12 before folate to avoid precipitating subacute combined degeneration.

title: Autoimmune hepatitis – Type I antibodies
content: Type I: Anti-nuclear antibodies (ANA) and/or anti-smooth muscle antibodies (SMA). Affects both adults and children.

title: Autoimmune hepatitis – Type II antibodies
content: Type II: Anti-liver/kidney microsomal type 1 antibodies (LKM1). Affects children only.

title: Autoimmune hepatitis – Type III antibodies
content: Type III: Soluble liver-kidney antigen. Affects adults in middle-age.

title: Autoimmune hepatitis – Amenorrhoea
content: Amenorrhoea is a common feature.

title: Autoimmune hepatitis – Raised IgG
content: Raised IgG levels are characteristic.

title: Autoimmune hepatitis – Piecemeal necrosis
content: Liver biopsy shows inflammation extending beyond limiting plate (piecemeal necrosis) and bridging necrosis.

title: Autoimmune hepatitis – Liver transplant
content: Liver transplantation may be required in advanced disease.

title: Barrett's oesophagus – Metaplasia definition
content: Metaplasia of the lower oesophageal mucosa, with squamous epithelium replaced by columnar epithelium.

title: Barrett's oesophagus – Cancer risk
content: 50-100 fold increased risk of oesophageal adenocarcinoma.

title: Barrett's oesophagus – Short vs long
content: Short Barrett's is less than 3cm, long Barrett's is greater than 3cm. Length correlates with chances of identifying metaplasia.

title: Barrett's oesophagus – Prevalence
content: Overall prevalence may be around 1 in 20, identified in up to 12% of those undergoing endoscopy for reflux.

title: Barrett's oesophagus – Histology
content: Columnar epithelium may resemble cardiac region of stomach or small intestine (with goblet cells, brush border).

title: Barrett's oesophagus – GORD strongest risk
content: GORD is the single strongest risk factor.

title: Barrett's oesophagus – Male predominance
content: Male gender (7:1 ratio).

title: Barrett's oesophagus – Smoking risk
content: Smoking is a risk factor.

title: Barrett's oesophagus – Central obesity risk
content: Central obesity is a risk factor.

title: Barrett's oesophagus – Alcohol not independent
content: Alcohol does not seem to be an independent risk factor.

title: Barrett's oesophagus – Asymptomatic
content: Barrett's oesophagus itself is asymptomatic but patients often have coexistent GORD symptoms.

title: Barrett's oesophagus – High-dose PPI
content: High-dose proton pump inhibitor is commonly used.

title: Barrett's oesophagus – PPI evidence limited
content: Evidence that PPIs reduce progression to dysplasia or induce regression is limited.

title: Barrett's oesophagus – Surveillance interval
content: For patients with metaplasia (but not dysplasia), endoscopy is recommended every 3-5 years.

title: Barrett's oesophagus – Radiofrequency ablation
content: Radiofrequency ablation is preferred first-line treatment for dysplasia, particularly low-grade.

title: Barrett's oesophagus – Endoscopic mucosal resection
content: Endoscopic mucosal resection is an option for dysplasia.

title: Bile-acid malabsorption – Definition
content: Cause of chronic diarrhoea due to excessive bile acid production (primary) or reduced absorption (secondary).

title: Bile-acid malabsorption – Steatorrhoea
content: Can lead to steatorrhoea and fat-soluble vitamin (A, D, E, K) malabsorption.

title: Bile-acid malabsorption – Ileal disease
content: Secondary causes often seen in patients with ileal disease such as Crohn's.

title: Bile-acid malabsorption – Cholecystectomy
content: Cholecystectomy is a secondary cause.

title: Bile-acid malabsorption – SIBO
content: Small intestinal bacterial overgrowth is a secondary cause.

title: Bile-acid malabsorption – SeHCAT test
content: SeHCAT is the test of choice. Nuclear medicine test using selenium homocholic acid taurine with scans 7 days apart.

title: Bile-acid malabsorption – Cholestyramine treatment
content: Bile acid sequestrants (e.g., cholestyramine) are used for management.

title: Bilirubin – Heme breakdown
content: Bilirubin is a by-product of heme breakdown from red blood cells and hepatic heme-containing proteins.

title: Bilirubin – Unconjugated form
content: Unconjugated bilirubin is bound to albumin in blood and taken up by hepatocytes for conjugation.

title: Bilirubin – Conjugation
content: Conjugation in hepatocytes renders bilirubin water-soluble for excretion into bile.

title: Bilirubin – Intestinal processing
content: Bacterial proteases produce urobilinogen from bilirubin; majority forms urobilin and stercobilin excreted in faeces.

title: Bilirubin – Enterohepatic circulation
content: Around 10% of bilirubin re-enters portal circulation and is excreted via kidneys in urine.

title: Bilirubin – Haemolysis cause
content: Raised unconjugated bilirubin occurs with haemolysis (pre-hepatic source).

title: Gilbert's syndrome – Mild deficiency
content: Mild glucuronyl transferase deficiency results in Gilbert's syndrome.

title: Crigler-Najjar – Moderate to severe
content: Moderate to severe glucuronyl transferase deficiency seen in Crigler-Najjar syndrome types I and II.

title: Neonatal jaundice – Transient deficiency
content: Transient glucuronyl transferase deficiency contributes to physiological neonatal jaundice.

title: Conjugated bilirubin – Dubin-Johnson
content: Raised conjugated bilirubin from defective excretion in Dubin-Johnson syndrome.

title: Jaundice – Threshold
content: Jaundice appears when bilirubin exceeds 35 μmol/L.

title: Cholestasis – Physical causes
content: Physical causes of cholestasis include gallstones, pancreatic and cholangiocarcinoma.

title: Cholestasis – Functional causes
content: Functional causes include drug-induced, pregnancy-related, and post-operative cholestasis.

title: Budd-Chiari – Definition
content: Hepatic vein thrombosis, usually in context of haematological disease or procoagulant condition.

title: Budd-Chiari – Polycythaemia cause
content: Polycythaemia rubra vera is a cause.

title: Budd-Chiari – Thrombophilia causes
content: Thrombophilia: activated protein C resistance, antithrombin III deficiency, protein C and S deficiencies.

title: Budd-Chiari – Pregnancy cause
content: Pregnancy is a cause.

title: Budd-Chiari – OCP cause
content: Combined oral contraceptive pill accounts for around 20% of cases.

title: Budd-Chiari – Classic triad
content: Classic triad: sudden onset severe abdominal pain, ascites with abdominal distension, and tender hepatomegaly.

title: Budd-Chiari – Doppler ultrasound
content: Ultrasound with Doppler flow studies is very sensitive and should be the initial radiological investigation.

title: Carcinoid syndrome – Liver metastases

title: Carcinoid syndrome – Diarrhoea feature

title: Carcinoid syndrome – Hypotension

title: Carcinoid syndrome – Heart valve disease

title: Carcinoid syndrome – ACTH secretion
