title: Carcinoid syndrome – Pellagra
content: Pellagra (niacin deficiency) can develop as dietary tryptophan is diverted to serotonin.

title: Carcinoid syndrome – 5-HIAA test
content: Urinary 5-HIAA is used for investigation.

title: Carcinoid syndrome – Chromogranin A
content: Plasma chromogranin A is used for investigation.

title: Carcinoid syndrome – Octreotide
content: Somatostatin analogues (e.g., octreotide) are used for management.

title: Carcinoid syndrome – Cyproheptadine
content: Cyproheptadine may help with diarrhoea.

title: Cholestyramine – Mechanism
content: Bile acid sequestrant that decreases bile acid reabsorption in small intestine, upregulating cholesterol conversion to bile acid.

title: Cholestyramine – LDL reduction
content: Main effect is to reduce LDL cholesterol.

title: Cholestyramine – Crohn's use
content: Occasionally used in Crohn's disease for diarrhoea following bowel resection.

title: Cholestyramine – Abdominal cramps
content: Adverse effects include abdominal cramps and constipation.

title: Cholestyramine – Fat-soluble vitamins
content: Decreases absorption of fat-soluble vitamins.

title: Cholestyramine – Gallstones
content: May cause cholesterol gallstones.

title: Cholestyramine – Triglycerides
content: May raise level of triglycerides.

title: C. difficile – Gram positive rod
content: Gram positive rod producing exotoxin causing intestinal damage and pseudomembranous colitis.

title: C. difficile – Broad-spectrum antibiotics
content: Develops when normal gut flora suppressed by broad-spectrum antibiotics.

title: C. difficile – Cephalosporins leading cause
content: Second and third-generation cephalosporins are now the leading cause.

title: C. difficile – Clindamycin historical
content: Clindamycin is historically associated but aetiology has evolved.

title: C. difficile – PPI risk factor
content: Proton pump inhibitors are a risk factor.

title: C. difficile – Spore-forming
content: Anaerobic gram-positive, spore-forming, toxin-producing bacillus.

title: C. difficile – Faecal-oral transmission
content: Transmission via faecal-oral route by ingestion of spores.

title: C. difficile – Toxins A and B
content: Releases two exotoxins (toxin A and toxin B) that act on intestinal epithelial cells and inflammatory cells.

title: C. difficile – Raised WCC
content: A raised white blood cell count is characteristic.

title: C. difficile – Toxic megacolon
content: If severe, toxic megacolon may develop.

title: C. difficile – Severity mild
content: Mild: Normal WCC, typically 3-5 loose stools per day.

title: C. difficile – Severity moderate
content: Moderate: Raised WCC (less than 15 × 10⁹/L).

title: C. difficile – Severity severe
content: Severe: WCC greater than 15 × 10⁹/L, or acutely raised creatinine (greater than 50% above baseline), or temperature greater than 38.5°C, or evidence of severe colitis.

title: C. difficile – Life-threatening features
content: Life-threatening: Hypotension, partial or complete ileus, toxic megacolon, or CT evidence of severe disease.

title: C. difficile – Toxin detection
content: Diagnosis made by detecting C. difficile toxin (CDT) in stool.

title: C. difficile – Antigen vs toxin
content: C. difficile antigen positivity shows exposure to bacteria, not current infection.

title: C. difficile – Review antibiotics
content: Current antibiotic therapy should be reviewed and stopped if possible.

title: C. difficile – First-line vancomycin
content: First-line therapy is oral vancomycin for 10 days.

title: C. difficile – Second-line fidaxomicin
content: Second-line therapy is oral fidaxomicin.

title: C. difficile – Third-line combination
content: Third-line therapy is oral vancomycin +/- IV metronidazole.

title: C. difficile – Recurrence rate
content: Recurrent infection occurs in around 20% of patients, increasing to 50% after second episode.

title: C. difficile – Recurrence within 12 weeks
content: Within 12 weeks of symptom resolution: oral fidaxomicin.

title: C. difficile – Recurrence after 12 weeks
content: After 12 weeks of symptom resolution: oral vancomycin OR fidaxomicin.

title: C. difficile – Life-threatening treatment
content: Life-threatening infection: oral vancomycin AND IV metronidazole. Surgery may be considered.

title: C. difficile – Bezlotoxumab
content: Bezlotoxumab is a monoclonal antibody targeting C. difficile toxin B. NICE do not support its use as not cost-effective.

title: C. difficile – Faecal transplant
content: Faecal microbiota transplant may be considered for patients with 2 or more previous episodes.

title: C. difficile – Isolation requirement
content: Isolation in side room until no diarrhoea (Bristol Stool Chart types 5-7) for at least 48 hours.

title: C. difficile – PPE requirements
content: All staff should wear disposable gloves and apron during contact with patients.

title: C. difficile – Hand washing essential
content: Hand washing is essential - alcohol gel does not kill C. difficile spores.

title: Coeliac disease – Prevalence
content: Affects around 1% of the UK population.

title: Coeliac disease – HLA-DQ2
content: Strongly associated with HLA-DQ2 (95% of patients).

title: Coeliac disease – HLA-DQ8
content: Associated with HLA-DQ8 (80% of patients).

title: Coeliac disease – Dermatitis herpetiformis
content: Associated with dermatitis herpetiformis (vesicular, pruritic skin eruption).

title: Coeliac disease – Chronic diarrhoea screening
content: Chronic or intermittent diarrhoea is an indication for screening.

title: Coeliac disease – Failure to thrive
content: Failure to thrive or faltering growth in children is an indication for screening.

title: Coeliac disease – Persistent GI symptoms
content: Persistent or unexplained gastrointestinal symptoms including nausea and vomiting are indications for screening.

title: Coeliac disease – Prolonged fatigue
content: Prolonged fatigue ('tired all the time') is an indication for screening.

title: Coeliac disease – Recurrent abdominal pain
content: Recurrent abdominal pain, cramping or distension are indications for screening.

title: Coeliac disease – Unexpected weight loss
content: Sudden or unexpected weight loss is an indication for screening.

title: Coeliac disease – Iron deficiency
content: Unexplained iron-deficiency anaemia is an indication for screening.

title: Coeliac disease – Folate more common
content: Folate deficiency is more common than vitamin B12 deficiency in coeliac disease.

title: Coeliac disease – Hyposplenism complication
content: Hyposplenism is a complication.

title: Coeliac disease – Osteoporosis
content: Osteoporosis and osteomalacia are complications.

title: Coeliac disease – Lactose intolerance
content: Lactose intolerance is a complication.

title: Coeliac disease – T-cell lymphoma
content: Enteropathy-associated T-cell lymphoma of small intestine is a complication.

title: Coeliac disease – Subfertility
content: Subfertility and unfavourable pregnancy outcomes are complications.

title: Coeliac disease – Oesophageal cancer risk
content: Rare: oesophageal cancer and other malignancies.

title: Coeliac disease – TTG first-choice
content: Tissue transglutaminase (TTG) antibodies (IgA) are first-choice according to NICE.

title: Coeliac disease – Endomyseal antibody
content: Endomyseal antibody (IgA) is used for diagnosis.

title: Coeliac disease – IgA deficiency test
content: Need to test for selective IgA deficiency, which would give false negative coeliac result.

title: Coeliac disease – IgG if IgA deficient
content: If IgA deficiency, test for IgG endomyseal antibodies, IgG deamidated gliadin peptide (DGP), or IgG transglutaminase antibodies.

title: Coeliac disease – Anti-gliadin not recommended
content: Anti-gliadin antibody (IgA or IgG) tests are not recommended by NICE.

title: Coeliac disease – Reintroduce gluten
content: If patients taking gluten-free diet, reintroduce gluten for at least 6 weeks prior to testing.

title: Coeliac disease – Biopsy gold standard
content: Endoscopic intestinal biopsy is the gold standard for diagnosis.

title: Coeliac disease – Duodenal biopsy
content: Traditionally done in duodenum but jejunal biopsies also sometimes performed.

title: Coeliac disease – Villous atrophy finding
content: Villous atrophy is a finding supportive of coeliac disease.

title: Coeliac disease – Crypt hyperplasia finding
content: Crypt hyperplasia is a finding supportive of coeliac disease.

title: Coeliac disease – Intraepithelial lymphocytes
content: Increase in intraepithelial lymphocytes is a finding supportive of coeliac disease.

title: Coeliac disease – Lamina propria infiltration
content: Lamina propria infiltration with lymphocytes is a finding supportive of coeliac disease.

title: Coeliac disease – Gluten-free diet
content: Management involves a gluten-free diet.

title: Coeliac disease – Wheat contains gluten
content: Wheat (bread, pasta, pastry) contains gluten.

title: Coeliac disease – Barley contains gluten
content: Barley (beer) contains gluten.

title: Coeliac disease – Whisky safe
content: Whisky is made using malted barley but proteins removed during distillation, making it safe.

title: Coeliac disease – Rye contains gluten
content: Rye contains gluten.

title: Coeliac disease – Oats tolerance
content: Some patients appear able to tolerate oats.

title: Coeliac disease – Rice gluten-free
content: Rice is gluten-free.

title: Coeliac disease – Potatoes gluten-free
content: Potatoes are gluten-free.

title: Coeliac disease – Corn gluten-free
content: Corn (maize) is gluten-free.

title: Coeliac disease – TTG compliance check
content: Tissue transglutaminase antibodies may be checked to monitor compliance with gluten-free diet.

title: Coeliac disease – Pneumococcal vaccine
content: All patients offered pneumococcal vaccine due to functional hyposplenism.

title: Coeliac disease – Vaccine booster 5 years
content: Coeliac UK recommends pneumococcal booster every 5 years.

title: Coeliac disease – Influenza individual basis
content: Influenza vaccine given on individual basis.

title: Colorectal cancer – Sporadic 95%
content: Sporadic colon cancer accounts for 95% of cases.

title: Colorectal cancer – HNPCC 5%
content: Hereditary non-polyposis colorectal carcinoma (HNPCC) accounts for 5% of cases.

title: Colorectal cancer – FAP less than 1%
content: Familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP) accounts for less than 1% of cases.

title: Colorectal cancer – APC gene loss
content: More than half of sporadic colon cancers show allelic loss of the APC gene.

title: Colorectal cancer – K-ras activation
content: Activation of K-ras oncogene contributes to invasive carcinoma.

title: Colorectal cancer – p53 deletion
content: Deletion of p53 and DCC tumour suppressor genes leads to invasive carcinoma.

title: HNPCC – Lynch syndrome
content: HNPCC (Lynch syndrome) is an autosomal dominant condition and most common form of inherited colon cancer.

title: HNPCC – Cancer development rate
content: Around 70-80% of HNPCC patients develop cancers.

title: HNPCC – Proximal colon
content: Cancers often affect proximal colon and are poorly differentiated and highly aggressive.

title: HNPCC – MSH2 mutation
content: MSH2 mutation accounts for 60% of HNPCC cases.

title: HNPCC – MLH1 mutation
content: MLH1 mutation accounts for 30% of HNPCC cases.

title: HNPCC – DNA mismatch repair
content: Mutations affect genes involved in DNA mismatch repair leading to microsatellite instability.

title: HNPCC – Endometrial cancer risk
content: Patients at higher risk of endometrial cancer, next most common association after colon cancer.

title: HNPCC – Amsterdam criteria
content: Amsterdam criteria: at least 3 family members with colon cancer, spanning at least 2 generations, at least one case before age 50.

title: FAP – Autosomal dominant
content: FAP is a rare autosomal dominant condition.

title: FAP – Hundreds of polyps
content: Leads to formation of hundreds of polyps by age 30-40 years.

title: FAP – Inevitable carcinoma
content: Patients inevitably develop carcinoma.

title: FAP – APC gene chromosome 5
content: Due to mutation in adenomatous polyposis coli gene (APC) on chromosome 5.

title: FAP – Genetic testing
content: Genetic testing done by analysing DNA from white blood cells.

title: FAP – Proctocolectomy in twenties
content: Patients generally have total proctocolectomy with IPAA formation in their twenties.

title: FAP – Duodenal tumour risk
content: Patients at risk from duodenal tumours.

title: Gardner's syndrome – FAP variant
content: Gardner's syndrome is a variant of FAP with osteomas of skull and mandible, retinal pigmentation, thyroid carcinoma, and epidermoid cysts.

title: Constipation – Definition detailed
content: Defecation that is unsatisfactory because of infrequent stools (less than 3 times weekly), difficult stool passage (with straining or discomfort), or seemingly incomplete defecation.

title: Constipation – Infrequent hard stools
content: The passage of infrequent hard stools is the main feature.

title: Constipation – Exclude secondary causes
content: Investigate and exclude any secondary causes, consider red flag symptoms.

title: Constipation – Exclude impaction
content: Exclude any faecal impaction.

title: Constipation – Increase fibre
content: Advice on increasing dietary fibre.

title: Constipation – Adequate fluids
content: Ensure adequate fluid intake.

title: Constipation – Activity levels
content: Ensure adequate activity levels.

title: Constipation – Bulk-forming first-line
content: First-line laxative is bulk-forming laxative such as ispaghula.

title: Constipation – Osmotic second-line
content: Second-line is osmotic laxative such as macrogol.

title: Constipation – Overflow diarrhoea
content: Overflow diarrhoea is a complication.

title: Constipation – Urinary retention
content: Acute urinary retention is a complication.

title: Constipation – Haemorrhoids complication
content: Haemorrhoids are a complication.

title: Crohn's disease – Genetic susceptibility
content: Strong genetic susceptibility but cause unknown.

title: Crohn's disease – Transmural inflammation
content: Inflammation occurs in all layers down to serosa.

title: Crohn's disease – Strictures fistulas adhesions
content: Transmural inflammation causes patients to be prone to strictures, fistulas, and adhesions.

title: Crohn's disease – 80% small bowel
content: 80% of patients have small bowel involvement, usually ileum, with 30% having ileitis exclusively.

title: Crohn's disease – 50% ileocolitis
content: 50% of patients have ileocolitis.

title: Crohn's disease – 20% colitis only
content: 20% of patients have colitis exclusively.

title: Crohn's disease – 30% perianal
content: 30% of patients have perianal disease.

title: Crohn's disease – Late adolescence onset
content: Typically presents in late adolescence or early adulthood.

title: Crohn's disease – Non-specific symptoms
content: May present with non-specific symptoms such as weight loss and lethargy.

title: Crohn's disease – Diarrhoea prominent adult
content: Diarrhoea is the most prominent symptom in adults.

title: Crohn's disease – Bloody diarrhoea colitis
content: Crohn's colitis may cause bloody diarrhoea.

title: Crohn's disease – Pain prominent child
content: Abdominal pain is the most prominent symptom in children.

title: Crohn's disease – Skin tags ulcers
content: Perianal disease includes skin tags or ulcers.

title: Crohn's disease – Extra-intestinal colitis
content: Extra-intestinal features more common in patients with colitis or perianal disease.

title: Crohn's disease – Raised inflammatory markers
content: Raised inflammatory markers are found.

title: Crohn's disease – Faecal calprotectin
content: Increased faecal calprotectin is found.

title: Crohn's disease – Low B12 and D
content: Low vitamin B12 and vitamin D are found.

title: Crohn's disease – CRP correlates
content: C-reactive protein correlates well with disease activity.

title: Crohn's disease – Colonoscopy choice
content: Colonoscopy is the investigation of choice.

title: Crohn's disease – Deep ulcers skip lesions
content: Features suggestive of Crohn's include deep ulcers and skip lesions.

title: Crohn's disease – Transmural histology
content: Histology shows inflammation in all layers from mucosa to serosa.

title: Crohn's disease – Goblet cells
content: Goblet cells are seen on histology.

title: Crohn's disease – Granulomas
content: Granulomas are seen on histology.

title: Crohn's disease – Kantor's string sign
content: Small bowel enema shows strictures with 'Kantor's string sign'.

title: Crohn's disease – Proximal bowel dilation
content: Proximal bowel dilation is seen on small bowel enema.

title: Crohn's disease – Rose thorn ulcers
content: 'Rose thorn' ulcers are seen on small bowel enema.

title: Crohn's disease – Fistulae on imaging
content: Fistulae may be seen on small bowel enema.

title: Crohn's disease – Stop smoking priority
content: Patients should be strongly advised to stop smoking.

title: Crohn's disease – NSAIDs may relapse
content: Some studies suggest increased risk of relapse secondary to NSAIDs but evidence is patchy.

title: Crohn's disease – OCP may relapse
content: Some studies suggest increased risk of relapse secondary to combined oral contraceptive pill but evidence is patchy.

title: Crohn's disease – Glucocorticoids induce remission
content: Glucocorticoids (oral, topical, or intravenous) are generally used to induce remission.

title: Crohn's disease – Budesonide alternative
content: Budesonide is an alternative in a subgroup of patients.

title: Crohn's disease – Enteral feeding
content: Enteral feeding with elemental diet may be used to induce remission, particularly if concern about steroid side-effects.

title: Crohn's disease – 5-ASA second-line
content: 5-ASA drugs (e.g., mesalazine) are used second-line to glucocorticoids but not as effective.

title: Crohn's disease – Azathioprine add-on
content: Azathioprine or mercaptopurine may be used as add-on to induce remission but not as monotherapy.

title: Crohn's disease – Methotrexate alternative
content: Methotrexate is an alternative to azathioprine.

title: Crohn's disease – Infliximab refractory
content: Infliximab is useful in refractory disease and fistulating Crohn's.

title: Crohn's disease – Metronidazole perianal
content: Metronidazole is often used for isolated perianal disease.

title: Crohn's disease – Azathioprine maintain remission
content: Azathioprine or mercaptopurine is used first-line to maintain remission.

title: Crohn's disease – TPMT before azathioprine
content: TPMT activity should be assessed before starting azathioprine or mercaptopurine.

title: Crohn's disease – Methotrexate second-line maintain
content: Methotrexate is used second-line to maintain remission.

title: Crohn's disease – 80% surgery
content: Around 80% of patients will eventually have surgery.

title: Crohn's disease – Ileocaecal resection
content: Stricturing terminal ileal disease treated with ileocaecal resection.

title: Crohn's disease – Segmental resections
content: Segmental small bowel resections may be performed.

title: Crohn's disease – Stricturoplasty
content: Stricturoplasty is a surgical option.

title: Crohn's disease – MRI for fistulae
content: MRI is investigation of choice for suspected perianal fistulae.

title: Crohn's disease – Simple vs complex fistula
content: MRI determines if fistula is simple (low) or complex (high, passing through or above muscle layers).

title: Crohn's disease – Metronidazole symptomatic fistula
content: Patients with symptomatic perianal fistulae usually given oral metronidazole.

title: Crohn's disease – Anti-TNF for fistulae
content: Anti-TNF agents such as infliximab may be effective in closing and maintaining closure of perianal fistulas.

title: Crohn's disease – Draining seton
content: A draining seton is used for complex fistulae.

title: Crohn's disease – Seton definition
content: A seton is surgical thread left in fistula for several weeks to keep it open and prevent abscess formation.

title: Crohn's disease – Perianal abscess drainage
content: Perianal abscess requires incision and drainage combined with antibiotic therapy.

title: Crohn's disease – Small bowel cancer risk
content: Small bowel cancer risk (standard incidence ratio = 40).

title: Crohn's disease – Colorectal cancer risk lower
content: Colorectal cancer risk (standard incidence ratio = 2, less than ulcerative colitis).

title: Crohn's disease – Osteoporosis risk
content: Patients at risk of osteoporosis.

content: May be accompanied by abdominal pain or nausea/vomiting.

title: Antibiotic therapy – Diarrhoea
content: More common with broad-spectrum antibiotics.

title: Constipation – Overflow diarrhoea
content: History of alternating diarrhoea and constipation. May lead to faecal incontinence in elderly.

title: Coeliac – Children presentation
content: In children may present with failure to thrive, diarrhoea, and abdominal distension.

title: Coeliac – Adults presentation
content: In adults lethargy, anaemia, diarrhoea, and weight loss. Other autoimmune conditions may coexist.

title: Thyrotoxicosis – Diarrhoea
content: Thyrotoxicosis is associated with diarrhoea.

title: Laxative abuse – Diarrhoea
content: Laxative abuse causes diarrhoea.

title: Appendicitis – Diarrhoea
content: Appendicitis may be associated with diarrhoea.

title: Radiation enteritis – Diarrhoea
content: Radiation enteritis causes diarrhoea.

title: Diarrhoea – Stool culture indications
content: NICE recommend stool sample if: systemically unwell, blood/pus in stool, immunocompromised, recent antibiotics/PPI/hospital, recent foreign travel, or public health indication.

title: Diarrhoea – Bloods not routine
content: Bloods not routinely indicated.

title: Diarrhoea – Severe complications
content: If severe, may show acute kidney injury, hypokalaemia, hyponatraemia.

title: Diverticulosis – Extremely common
content: Extremely common disorder with multiple outpouchings of bowel wall, most commonly sigmoid colon.

title: Diverticulosis – Terminology
content: Diverticular disease is for symptomatic patients; diverticulosis is more accurate for diverticula being present.

title: Diverticulosis – Increasing age
content: Increasing age is a risk factor.

title: Diverticulosis – Low-fibre diet
content: Low-fibre diet is a risk factor.

title: Painful diverticular disease – Features
content: Altered bowel habit, colicky left sided abdominal pain. High fibre diet recommended.

title: Diverticulitis – Classical presentation
content: Left iliac fossa pain and tenderness, anorexia, nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea, features of infection.

title: Diverticulitis – Mild oral antibiotics
content: Mild attacks treated with oral antibiotics.

title: Diverticulitis – Severe hospital management
content: Significant episodes: nil by mouth, IV fluids, IV antibiotics (cephalosporin + metronidazole).

title: Diverticulitis – Abscess complication
content: Abscess formation is a complication.

title: Diverticulitis – Peritonitis complication
content: Peritonitis is a complication.

title: Diverticulitis – Obstruction complication
content: Obstruction is a complication.

content: Paracetamol, sodium valproate, phenytoin, MAOIs, halothane, anti-TB drugs, statins, alcohol, amiodarone, methyldopa, nitrofurantoin cause hepatocellular pattern.

content: OCP, flucloxacillin, co-amoxiclav, erythromycin, anabolic steroids, phenothiazines, sulphonylureas, fibrates cause cholestasis.

content: Methotrexate, methyldopa, amiodarone cause liver cirrhosis.

title: Dyspepsia – Urgent dysphagia
content: All patients with dysphagia need urgent referral.

title: Dyspepsia – Urgent upper abdominal mass

title: Dyspepsia – Non-urgent haematemesis
content: Patients with haematemesis need non-urgent referral.

title: Dyspepsia – Non-urgent age 55 resistant
content: Patients aged ≥55 with treatment-resistant dyspepsia need non-urgent referral.

title: Dyspepsia – Review medications
content: Review medications for possible causes of dyspepsia.

title: Dyspepsia – Lifestyle advice
content: Provide lifestyle advice.

content: Initial diagnosis: carbon-13 urea breath test or stool antigen test.

content: No need to check eradication if symptoms resolved following test and treat.

content: If repeat testing required, carbon-13 urea breath test should be used.

content: Dysphagia with weight loss, anorexia, or vomiting during eating. Past history of Barrett's, GORD, smoking, alcohol.

title: Oesophagitis – Dysphagia
content: History of heartburn. Odynophagia but no weight loss and systemically well.

content: History of HIV or risk factors such as steroid inhaler use.

title: Globus hystericus – Dysphagia

title: GORD – Endoscopy age over 55
content: Age greater than 55 years is an indication for upper GI endoscopy.

title: GORD – Endoscopy symptoms over 4 weeks

title: GORD – Endoscopy dysphagia
content: Dysphagia is an indication for upper GI endoscopy.

title: GORD – Endoscopy relapsing symptoms

title: GORD – Endoscopy weight loss
content: Weight loss is an indication.

title: GORD – Oesophagitis complication
content: Oesophagitis is a complication.

title: GORD – Ulcers complication

title: GORD – Anaemia complication

title: GORD – Benign strictures
content: Benign strictures are a complication.

title: GORD – Oesophageal carcinoma complication
content: Oesophageal carcinoma is a complication.

title: Gilbert's syndrome – Autosomal recessive
content: Autosomal recessive condition of defective bilirubin conjugation due to deficiency of UDP glucuronosyltransferase.

title: Gilbert's syndrome – Prevalence
content: Prevalence approximately 1-2% in general population.

title: Gilbert's syndrome – Unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia
content: Unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia (not in urine).

title: Gilbert's syndrome – Jaundice triggers
content: Jaundice may only be seen during intercurrent illness, exercise, or fasting.

title: Gilbert's syndrome – Genetic testing
content: Genetic testing for UGT1A1 promoter region polymorphism provides definitive diagnosis.

title: Gilbert's syndrome – No treatment
content: No treatment required.

title: Haemochromatosis – Chromosome 6
content: Caused by inheritance of mutations in HFE gene on both copies of chromosome 6.

title: Haemochromatosis – 1 in 10 carriers
content: 1 in 10 people of European descent carry a mutation in genes affecting iron metabolism, mainly HFE.

title: Haemochromatosis – 1 in 200 prevalence
content: Prevalence in people of European descent is 1 in 200, more common than cystic fibrosis.

title: Haemochromatosis – Early symptoms
content: Early symptoms include fatigue, erectile dysfunction, and arthralgia (often of hands).

title: Haemochromatosis – Hepatomegaly
content: Liver: stigmata of chronic liver disease, hepatomegaly, cirrhosis, hepatocellular deposition.

title: Haemochromatosis – Cardiac failure
content: Cardiac failure secondary to dilated cardiomyopathy.

title: Haemochromatosis – Hypogonadism
content: Hypogonadism secondary to cirrhosis and pituitary dysfunction (hypogonadotrophic hypogonadism).

title: Haemochromatosis – Hand arthritis
content: Arthritis especially of the hands.

title: Haemochromatosis – Reversible cardiomyopathy
content: Cardiomyopathy and skin pigmentation are reversible with treatment.

title: Haemochromatosis – Irreversible cirrhosis
content: Liver cirrhosis, diabetes mellitus, hypogonadotrophic hypogonadism, and arthropathy are irreversible.

title: Haemochromatosis – Transferrin saturation screening
content: Transferrin saturation is considered the most useful marker for screening general population.

title: Haemochromatosis – Ferritin not early
content: Ferritin should be measured but not usually abnormal in early stages of iron accumulation.

title: Haemochromatosis – Family genetic testing
content: Testing family members: genetic testing for HFE mutation.

title: Haemochromatosis – Transferrin over 55% men
content: Transferrin saturation greater than 55% in men or greater than 50% in women.

title: Haemochromatosis – Raised ferritin iron
content: Raised ferritin (e.g., greater than 500 μg/L) and iron.

title: Haemochromatosis – Low TIBC
content: Low TIBC.

title: Haemochromatosis – C282Y H63D mutations
content: Molecular genetic testing for C282Y and H63D mutations.

title: Haemochromatosis – MRI quantify iron
content: MRI is generally used to quantify liver and/or cardiac iron.

title: Haemochromatosis – Biopsy if cirrhosis
content: Liver biopsy now generally only used if suspected hepatic cirrhosis.

title: Haemochromatosis – Venesection first-line
content: Venesection is first-line treatment.

title: Haemochromatosis – Monitor transferrin ferritin
content: Monitoring: transferrin saturation below 50% and serum ferritin below 50 μg/L.

title: Haemochromatosis – Desferrioxamine second-line
content: Desferrioxamine may be used second-line.

title: Haemochromatosis – Desferrioxamine mechanism
content: Parenteral iron-chelating agent that binds free iron (Fe³⁺) to form ferrioxamine, excreted by kidneys.

title: Haemochromatosis – Desferrioxamine indications
content: Reserved for patients who cannot tolerate venesection (anaemia, poor venous access) or secondary haemochromatosis.

title: H. pylori – Gram-negative
content: Gram-negative bacteria associated with gastrointestinal problems, principally peptic ulcer disease.

title: H. pylori – Chemotaxis flagella
content: Chemotaxis away from low pH areas, using flagella to burrow into mucous lining.

title: H. pylori – Urease alkalinization
content: Secretes urease converting urea to NH3, alkalinizing acidic environment for increased survival.

title: H. pylori – CagA toxin
content: Releases bacterial cytotoxins (e.g., CagA toxin) disrupting gastric mucosa.

title: H. pylori – 95% duodenal ulcers
content: 95% of duodenal ulcers associated with H. pylori.

title: H. pylori – 75% gastric ulcers
content: 75% of gastric ulcers associated with H. pylori.

title: H. pylori – Gastric cancer association
content: Associated with gastric cancer.

title: H. pylori – MALT lymphoma
content: B cell lymphoma of MALT tissue (eradication causes regression in 80% of patients).

title: H. pylori – Atrophic gastritis
content: Associated with atrophic gastritis.

title: H. pylori – No role in GORD
content: No role in GORD for eradication of H. pylori.

title: H. pylori – First-line eradication
content: First-line: PPI + amoxicillin + (clarithromycin OR metronidazole) for 7 days.

title: H. pylori – Ongoing symptoms treatment
content: If ongoing symptoms: PPI + amoxicillin + (clarithromycin OR metronidazole, whichever not used first line).

title: H. pylori – Penicillin-allergic
content: If penicillin-allergic: PPI + metronidazole + clarithromycin.

title: H. pylori – Urea breath test procedure
content: Patients consume drink with carbon-13 enriched urea. Urea broken down by H. pylori urease. After 30 mins exhale into glass tube. Mass spectrometry calculates 13C CO2.

title: H. pylori – Urea breath timing
content: Should not be performed within 4 weeks of antibacterial or 2 weeks of antisecretory drug.

title: H. pylori – Urea breath sensitivity
content: Sensitivity 95-98%, specificity 97-98%.

title: H. pylori – Urea breath eradication check
content: May be used to check for H. pylori eradication.

title: H. pylori – Rapid urease test
content: Biopsy sample mixed with urea and pH indicator. Colour change if H. pylori urease activity. Sensitivity 90-95%, specificity 95-98%.

title: H. pylori – Serum antibody limitation
content: Remains positive after eradication. Sensitivity 85%, specificity 80%.

title: H. pylori – Culture sensitivity
content: Culture provides antibiotic sensitivity information. Sensitivity 70%, specificity 100%.

title: H. pylori – Gastric biopsy histology
content: Histological evaluation alone, no culture. Sensitivity 95-99%, specificity 95-99%.

title: H. pylori – Stool antigen test
content: Sensitivity 90%, specificity 95%.

title: Hepatic encephalopathy – Ammonia glutamine
content: Aetiology thought to include excess absorption of ammonia and glutamine from bacterial breakdown of proteins in gut.

title: Hepatic encephalopathy – Acute and chronic
content: May be seen with acute liver failure or chronic disease.

title: Hepatic encephalopathy – Minimal covert
content: Many patients with cirrhosis develop subtle symptoms like mild cognitive impairment before features become recognisable ('minimal' or 'covert' hepatic encephalopathy).

title: Hepatic encephalopathy – TIPSS precipitates
content: Transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunting (TIPSS) may precipitate encephalopathy.

title: Hepatic encephalopathy – Confusion altered GCS
content: Confusion, altered GCS.

title: Hepatic encephalopathy – Asterixis
content: Asterixis: 'liver flap', arrhythmic negative myoclonus with frequency of 3-5 Hz.

title: Hepatic encephalopathy – Constructional apraxia
content: Constructional apraxia: inability to draw 5-pointed star.

title: Hepatic encephalopathy – Triphasic waves
content: Triphasic slow waves on EEG.

title: Hepatic encephalopathy – Raised ammonia
content: Raised ammonia level (supportive but not diagnostic - levels do not correlate well with severity).

title: Hepatic encephalopathy – Grade I
content: Grade I: Irritability.

title: Hepatic encephalopathy – Grade II
content: Grade II: Confusion, inappropriate behaviour.

title: Hepatic encephalopathy – Grade III
content: Grade III: Incoherent, restless.

title: Hepatic encephalopathy – Grade IV
content: Grade IV: Coma.

title: Hepatic encephalopathy – SBP precipitant
content: Infection (e.g., spontaneous bacterial peritonitis) is a precipitating factor.

title: Hepatic encephalopathy – GI bleed precipitant
content: GI bleed is a precipitating factor.

title: Hepatic encephalopathy – Post-TIPSS
content: Post transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt is a precipitating factor.

title: Hepatic encephalopathy – Constipation precipitant
content: Constipation is a precipitating factor.

title: Hepatic encephalopathy – Drugs precipitant
content: Drugs (sedatives, diuretics) are precipitating factors.

title: Hepatic encephalopathy – Hypokalaemia precipitant
content: Hypokalaemia is a precipitating factor.

title: Hepatic encephalopathy – Renal failure precipitant
content: Renal failure is a precipitating factor.

title: Hepatic encephalopathy – Lactulose first-line
content: NICE recommend lactulose first-line, with addition of rifaximin for secondary prophylaxis.

title: Hepatic encephalopathy – Lactulose mechanism
content: Lactulose promotes excretion of ammonia and increases metabolism of ammonia by gut bacteria.

title: Hepatic encephalopathy – Rifaximin mechanism
content: Antibiotics such as rifaximin modulate gut flora resulting in decreased ammonia production.

title: Hepatic encephalopathy – Embolisation transplant
content: Other options include embolisation of portosystemic shunts and liver transplantation in selected patients.

title: Hepatitis B – HBsAg first marker
content: Surface antigen (HBsAg) is first marker to appear and causes production of anti-HBs.

title: Hepatitis B – HBsAg acute 1-6 months
content: HBsAg normally implies acute disease (present for 1-6 months).

title: Hepatitis B – HBsAg chronic over 6 months
content: If HBsAg present for greater than 6 months, implies chronic disease (infective).

title: Hepatitis B – Anti-HBs immunity
content: Anti-HBs implies immunity (either exposure or immunisation). Negative in chronic disease.

title: Hepatitis B – Anti-HBc previous infection
content: Anti-HBc implies previous (or current) infection. IgM anti-HBc appears during acute or recent infection for about 6 months. IgG anti-HBc persists.

title: Hepatitis B – HBeAg viral replication
content: HBeAg is protein from breakdown of hepatitis B core antigen. Presence indicates active viral replication and high infectivity.

title: Hepatitis B – Immunisation serology
content: Previous immunisation: anti-HBs positive, all others negative.

title: Hepatitis B – Previous not carrier
content: Previous hepatitis B (greater than 6 months ago), not carrier: anti-HBc positive, HBsAg negative.

title: Hepatitis B – Carrier serology
content: Previous hepatitis B, now carrier: anti-HBc positive, HBsAg positive.

title: Viral hepatitis – Nausea vomiting anorexia
content: Common symptoms include nausea and vomiting, anorexia.

title: Viral hepatitis – Myalgia
content: Myalgia is a common symptom.

title: Viral hepatitis – Lethargy
content: Lethargy is a common symptom.

title: Viral hepatitis – RUQ pain
content: Right upper quadrant pain is a common symptom.
